Guide

Security

This page is written for the reviewer deciding whether this SDK may go into a regulated application. Every control below names the file that enforces it, so the claim can be read against the source rather than taken on trust — and every control the SDK does not implement is listed as plainly as the ones it does.

One sentence summarises the design: the SDK is a confined WebView plus a versioned message channel. It holds a bearer token in memory, hands it to one origin over that channel, refuses to let the main frame leave that origin's /embed subtree, and gets out of the way. It stores nothing, mints nothing, and logs nothing sensitive.

  • SDK 1.0.0
  • Bridge protocol v1
  • MIT — source is public
  • Report: security@amthalgroup.com

Threat model and the trust boundary

Three parties share one screen: your application, the Amthal Client Portal running in an embedded WebView, and the network between them. The SDK exists to make the boundary between the first two explicit and narrow.

Who trusts what, and where that trust is enforced
Party Trusts Does not trust
Your app (the host) The portal origin it configured, and every script that origin serves. JavaScript runs on portal content, and iOS re-affirms that grant on the same decision that admits each allowlisted main-frame URL. Any other origin; any main-frame URL outside basePath + /embed; any bridge envelope whose v is not 1; the network.
The portal (the web layer) The host to supply a valid bearer token over the bridge, and to be a genuine Amthal host — on React Native the portal only speaks to a WebView that set window.__AMTHAL_EMBEDDED_RN__ before content load. A URL as a credential carrier — it never receives one that way; its own HTTP layer while form delegation is active.
Neither — Cleartext transport (rejected at config time), an unknown message type (ignored), a reply with no pending request (dropped), a message that already carries replyTo (never re-replied to).

The boundary in one sentence

The unit of trust is the origin, not the individual script. Once a page is served from the configured portal origin inside the embed subtree, the SDK treats everything running on it as the portal. That is the correct boundary for a WebView, and it is also the limit of what the SDK can enforce — see what this SDK does not do.

What is out of scope

SECURITY.md scopes this repository: the bridge protocol, the iOS and Android SDKs, and the React Native and Expo wrappers. The Client Portal deployment itself and the Optimum Core API behind it are out of scope here — they are operated per tenant, and issues in them go through your usual Amthal support contact, which reaches the same team. That matters for this review: the portal's own Content-Security-Policy, session lifetime, and API authorisation are tenant-side controls you should assess separately, against the deployment your app will actually point at.

How the bearer token travels, and where it never appears

Your app obtains the token with its own login flow; the SDK never mints, refreshes or stores one. It carries it across the boundary in exactly two message types and nowhere else.

The credential's complete itinerary
WherePresent?Detail
Bridge init payload Yes Sent as the reply to the portal's hello, re-sent on every subsequent hello (the handshake is idempotent).
Bridge auth payload Yes Re-issued at any time through updateAuth, or through the refresh function handed to onAuthExpired.
The loaded URL Never The main-frame URL is {baseUrl} plus a route such as /embed/form/internal/3021 — product and route values only.
Query string or fragment Never Android's PortalConfig constructor rejects a baseUrl carrying either; iOS drops any query or fragment while rebuilding the URL in portalURL(forPath:).
The manifest request Never GET {baseUrl}/embed/manifest.json is unauthenticated by design — iOS sets only a timeout and cache policy, Android only an Accept header.
SDK logs Never Diagnostics never include credentials, and download header values are never logged on any platform.
Download requests Conditionally Headers from a downloadRequest are attached only when the target URL passes the origin allowlist — see below.

The download header check

A downloadRequest message carries both a URL and a header map, and the portal chooses both. If the SDK attached those headers to whatever URL it was given, a compromised or buggy portal page could hand an Authorization header to a third-party host. Both native handlers make the same check before attaching anything: 

// ios/Sources/AmthalPortal/DownloadHandler.swift
if let headers = payload.headers, config.isOriginAllowed(url) {
    for (field, value) in headers { request.setValue(value, forHTTPHeaderField: field) }
}

// android/.../internal/DownloadHandler.kt
if (config.isUrlOriginAllowed(url)) {
    for ((key, value) in headers) conn.setRequestProperty(key, value)
}

An off-origin download still proceeds — without the headers. Both handlers also require an https scheme (or a loopback host, or an honoured development hatch) before the request is made at all.

React Native's default download path cannot attach headers at all

With no onDownloadRequest prop, the wrapper falls back to Linking.openURL(payload.url), which hands the URL to the system browser with no headers — so an authenticated download silently fails rather than leaking anything. If your forms produce authenticated attachments on React Native, you must supply onDownloadRequest and perform the fetch yourself, which makes the token your code's responsibility at that point.

In-memory handling, and accidental printing

The token lives in memory for the life of the session — in BridgeController.currentAuth on iOS, in the view's session state on Android, in a ref on React Native. It is never written to disk by the SDK.

Android's PortalAuth overrides toString() to redact all three fields, so a stray log line or crash report prints PortalAuth(token=***, …). The Swift PortalAuth has no such override — it is a plain struct, so print(auth) or string interpolation in your own code will print the token verbatim. That is a real difference between the platforms, and it is your code, not the SDK's, that decides whether it matters.

Main-frame navigation confinement

The single most important runtime control. A main-frame navigation is allowed if and only if both conditions hold:

  1. its origin is on the allowlist — the baseUrl host plus anything in allowedOrigins — over https (or http for a loopback host, or under an honoured development hatch); and
  2. its path is inside the embed subtree, computed as basePath + "/embed", where basePath is the path component of your baseUrl.

The second half is why the deploy path prefix is not optional. A portal served under /portal/ has basePath = "/portal" and a boundary of /portal/embed; testing against a literal /embed would reject every real URL. The check is a shared helper (isEmbedPath) mirrored by hand in each host, and it matches the prefix exactly or the prefix followed by / — so /portal/embedded-elsewhere is outside.

Where confinement is enforced, per host
HostEnforcement pointBlocked navigation becomes
React Native onShouldStartLoadWithRequest returns false onOpenExternal if you supplied one, otherwise Linking.openURL
iOS & Expo WKNavigationDelegate.decidePolicyFor navigationAction answers .cancel The delegate's openExternal(url:), otherwise SFSafariViewController for http(s) and UIApplication.open for anything else
Android WebViewClient.shouldOverrideUrlLoading returns true AmthalPortalListener.onOpenExternal, otherwise an ACTION_VIEW intent hinted as a Custom Tab

On iOS the allow branch also re-affirms preferences.allowsContentJavaScript = true per navigation, so content JavaScript is granted on the same decision that admits the URL — the two cannot drift apart.

Sub-frames are deliberately exempt

Only the main frame is confined. A legitimate page loads third-party sub-frames — reCAPTCHA, payment widgets, embedded maps — and cancelling one of those does not protect anybody: it externalises a fragment of a page, so the user lands in Safari on google.com/recaptcha/api2/anchor and the form is left behind. This is a stated design decision in the protocol, not an oversight.

React Native has to detect sub-frames from two signals, because neither is reliable alone: isTopFrame === false, or an iOS-only mainDocumentURL that differs from the URL being requested. A request matching either is allowed through as a sub-frame.

Two things a reviewer should notice about the boundary

The openExternal URL is not scheme-filtered. A blocked navigation, a target=_blank, or a portal-sent openExternal message is handed to the platform opener as-is — including custom schemes. Your onOpenExternal / delegate hook is the interception point, and returning true from it stops the SDK opening anything. If your threat model includes a compromised portal page driving intents, implement that hook and allow-list schemes there.

The allowlist compares hosts on the native SDKs and full origins on React Native. iOS and Android match the host case-insensitively (Android strips any port from allowedOrigins entries); the React Native wrapper compares the complete scheme://host:port string. A non-default port therefore behaves differently across hosts — on React Native it must be spelled out in allowedOrigins.

On React Native, originWhitelist is not the boundary

The wrapper sets originWhitelist={['http://*', 'https://*']} deliberately. react-native-webview consults that list first and, on a miss, hands the URL straight to Linking.openURL without calling the SDK's handler — and it does not distinguish main frame from sub-frame, so a narrow whitelist throws every third-party sub-resource at the system browser. Confinement is done in onShouldStartLoadWithRequest, which knows about sub-frames and cancels rather than externalises an off-subtree main frame. Judge the boundary there, not on the whitelist prop.

Origin checking on every message and every evaluation

Confinement stops the main frame moving. The origin checks stop the bridge being used from, or pointed at, a page that is not the portal — in both directions, on every single message.

Origin gates, per direction and host
DirectionReact NativeiOS & ExpoAndroid
Inbound (web → native) The message event's own url is compared against the allowed origins; a mismatch is dropped. Two gates. The WebView's current URL must be allowlisted, and message.frameInfo.securityOrigin.host — the posting frame itself — must be allowlisted. config.isUrlOriginAllowed(webView.url) is checked on the main thread before the envelope is even parsed.
Outbound (native → web) The last known main-frame URL is checked before every injectJavaScript. config.isOriginAllowed(webView.url) before every evaluateJavaScript; the send is dropped, not queued. isCurrentOriginAllowed() before every evaluateJavascript; suppressed sends are logged, not retried.

The outbound check is the one that protects the credential: init and auth are ordinary outbound messages, so a WebView that has somehow left the portal origin receives nothing at all. On React Native the comparison uses the last URL reported by the navigation-state callback; before the first such report there is no value to compare and the send proceeds — a window that covers the initial load of the URL the SDK itself constructed.

Envelope-level rules

Every host applies the same parsing discipline, and each rule is a silent drop rather than an error — forward compatibility is a protocol requirement, so a newer portal cannot break an older app by sending something it does not recognise.

ConditionBehaviour
v is not 1Silently ignored.
Unparseable JSONSilently ignored.
Unknown typeIgnored — never treated as an error.
Unknown payload fieldsIgnored.
replyTo matches no pending requestDropped; an ack is never re-replied to.
Any request with no answerResolves to its safe default — backPressed to handled:false, dismissRequested to dirty:false — after the protocol timeout.
What origin checking cannot do: it separates origins, not scripts

The bridge hooks are page-world globals by necessity — window.webkit.messageHandlers.amthal on iOS (registered in contentWorld: .page), the __amthalAndroid JavaScript interface on Android, window.ReactNativeWebView.postMessage on React Native — and the inbound channel is window.__amthalReceive, which the portal defines.

Any script executing on the portal origin can therefore post bridge messages and can hook __amthalReceive to observe the init payload. Script injection in the portal is token compromise, and no native-side check can prevent that. The defence is portal-side — its Content-Security-Policy, its output encoding, its dependency hygiene — and it lives in a different repository, on a deployment your tenant operates. Review it there; do not assume this page covers it.

TLS, cleartext, and the allowInsecureHttp development hatch

HTTPS is required, and the requirement is applied at configuration time — before any request leaves the device. Plain http is accepted only for loopback hosts, or through a development hatch that a release build cannot honour.

What each host does with a cleartext base URL
HostGate on the hatchRelease behaviour
React Native __DEV__ Refused before the manifest fetch — loadFailed with "Insecure baseUrl rejected".
iOS #if DEBUG inside PortalConfig The requested flag is discarded by the compiler (honourInsecureHTTP returns false outside DEBUG), so the initialiser throws PortalConfigError.insecureBaseURL.
Expo #if DEBUG in the native module Forced to false while the JS options are parsed, before PortalConfig is built.
Android The app's own FLAG_DEBUGGABLE Ignored with a Logcat warning, and beginLoad() refuses the load through isBaseUrlTransportAllowed(context) — the single funnel for the first load and every retry.

The Android split is worth understanding precisely, because it is the one platform where the config object alone is not the whole answer. PortalConfig is plain data with no Context, so its constructor accepts a cleartext URL whenever the flag was passed; isBaseUrlTransportAllowed(context) is the check that decides whether the request may leave the device, and the view makes it before every load. A release APK cannot be talked into cleartext by one boolean in the embedding code.

The flag alone was never sufficient

The platform still has to permit cleartext: an App Transport Security exception in Info.plist on iOS, a network_security_config on Android. Both belong in a debug source set only, and both are things to grep for in the release configuration — see the checklist.

Certificate pinning

Android only, and partial. PortalConfig.certificatePinner is an optional ((X509Certificate) -> Boolean) invoked with the server's leaf certificate; returning false throws and aborts the transfer. There is no equivalent on React Native, Expo or iOS.

CoversSDK-initiated HTTPS only: the manifest fetch and SDK downloads.
Does not coverThe portal page load and everything the page then fetches — those go through the system WebView network stack, which exposes no pinning hook on any platform.
TimingThe hook runs against an established connection: verifyPinning reads serverCertificates after conn.connect(). The handshake completes before the check, which then aborts the transfer.

Treat it as defence in depth for two specific requests, not as pinning for the session. If your policy requires pinned transport for everything the app renders, pin at the network edge; this SDK cannot give you that property inside a system WebView, and does not claim to.

WebView hardening

The same posture is applied on all four hosts, by construction rather than by configuration — none of these is an option you can turn back on through the public API.

Settings applied to the portal WebView
SettingReact NativeiOS & ExpoAndroid
File access from the pageOffOff (no file URLs loaded)Off
Universal access from file URLsOffn/aOff (content access off)
Mixed contentneverBlocked by WebKitMIXED_CONTENT_NEVER_ALLOW
Multiple windows / window.openOffOff — routed to the external openerOff
Link previewOffOffn/a
Back/forward gesturesOffOffn/a
GeolocationNot requestedNot requestedDisabled, and prompts auto-denied
Camera / microphone permissionRequestPlatform defaultPlatform defaultDenied
Media autoplayRequires gestureInline playback enabled; autoplay follows the WebKit defaultRequires gesture
Safe BrowsingPlatform defaultPlatform defaultAsserted where supported

Two structural points behind the table. The bridge transport is installed before any content loads — a WKUserScript at document start, an addJavascriptInterface call before loadUrl, injectedJavaScriptBeforeContentLoaded on React Native — which is what lets the portal buffer its hello and is also why exactly one interface is exposed. And the version handshake runs before the page is loaded at all: the manifest's bridgeProtocolVersion must equal 1, its portalVersion must satisfy your minPortalVersion, and the SDK's own version must satisfy the manifest's minSdkVersion. A mismatched pairing never reaches a render.

Logging, and what a release build drops

The portal can send log messages over the bridge, and the WebView produces console output. The protocol requires both to be dropped in release builds. Here is exactly how each host implements that, including the one place where the gate is weaker than the sentence above suggests.

Diagnostics gating, per host
HostBridge log messagesWebView inspection
React Native Requires __DEV__ and enableLogging. A release bundle prints nothing whatever the flag says. webviewDebuggingEnabled follows __DEV__, independent of enableLogging.
iOS & Expo Wrapped in #if DEBUG and gated on enableLogging; the code is not compiled into a release build. isInspectable is set only inside #if DEBUG, and only when enableLogging is true.
Android Gated on enableLogging only. There is no build-type check on this path, so a release APK built with enableLogging = true will write portal log messages and WebView console output to Logcat. The SDK never calls setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled — inspection follows whatever the host app sets.
Android: drive enableLogging from your own debug constant

This is the one platform where the flag is load-bearing in a release build. Set it from BuildConfig.DEBUG — never a literal true, and never a remote configuration value. What reaches Logcat is portal-authored log text and page console output, which the SDK does not inspect or redact.

Independently of the flag, the SDK's own diagnostics never contain credentials, and download header values are never logged on any platform — both handlers say so in the code and neither formats the header map into a message. Anything you log on top of the SDK is yours to keep clean: a bearer token on a log line is a bearer token in a crash report.

What destroy() clears — and what it cannot guarantee

Teardown is a best-effort protocol exchange, not a transaction. Saying so precisely matters more here than anywhere else on this page, because "the session is cleared" is the kind of sentence a reviewer is entitled to test.

The sequence

  1. Native sends destroy

    On unmount, on view destruction, or when the host dismisses the sheet. The message goes through the same outbound origin check as any other.

  2. The web side clears its persisted auth

    The portal drops its stored user object and branch id (USER_KEY, BRANCH_ID) on receipt, regardless of whether its acknowledgement ever gets back.

  3. Native waits one second, then releases

    A grace window for the ack, then the message handler or JavaScript interface is removed, loading is stopped, pending round-trips resolve to their defaults, and the WebView is released.

  4. Android additionally clears WebView storage

    WebStorage.deleteAllData() and CookieManager.removeAllCookies(), each wrapped in its own try/catch. Note the blast radius: the system WebView offers only app-global clearing, so this clears storage and cookies for every WebView in your app, not just the portal's. If your app has its own WebView session, that is a behaviour to test for.

Say this plainly: what destroy() does not guarantee

It is not acknowledged-delivery. The native side waits up to one second and then proceeds regardless. If the web layer was already gone — a crashed content process, a killed app, a device powered off mid-form — the message was never processed, and the portal's persisted auth is cleared only on its next load.

iOS and React Native do not clear WebView storage. Only the Android host does. The iOS SDK uses the default, persistent WKWebsiteDataStore and does not call removeData at teardown; the React Native wrapper sends destroy and nothing more. On those two platforms, clearing the portal origin's storage is the web side's job, and it happens only if the message arrived.

It does not clear files already written to disk. Downloads and camera captures survive teardown — see data at rest.

It cannot scrub memory. The token is an immutable Swift/Kotlin/JS string; copies may exist in the runtime's heap until collected, and a memory-dumping adversary with code execution on the device is outside what any of this defends against.

The practical consequence for your integration: logout is two actions, not one. Unmount the portal screen so destroy is sent, and discard your own stored token. A live SDK session beside a logged-out app is an application bug the SDK cannot detect.

Data at rest

The SDK writes four kinds of thing to durable storage. None of them is the token, and none of them is encrypted by the SDK.

Everything the SDK persists, and who cleans it up
WhatWhereCleared by
The portal's own session WebView storage for the portal origin — the portal persists its user object and branch id there, which is why destroy exists at all. The web side on destroy; additionally, app-globally, by Android's teardown.
Downloaded attachments iOS: NSTemporaryDirectory()/AmthalPortalDownloads.
Android: cacheDir/amthal-portal/, timestamp-prefixed and filename-sanitised, exposed to the viewer through a FileProvider with a read-only grant.		 Nothing. Files are deleted on failure only; a successful download stays until the OS reclaims the cache or your app clears it.
Camera captures for form uploads Android: cacheDir/amthal-portal-camera/, via FileProvider. Deleted when the user cancels the chooser; otherwise it stays for the OS to reclaim.
The pending-session handle Android only, and in memory: PortalSessionStore keeps config, request, auth and listener behind a UUID so the activity/fragment wrappers can pass a key rather than parcel a listener. Process death — deliberately. The session does not survive it, and the wrappers close themselves when the lookup fails.

Your token storage is yours. Keychain on iOS, Keystore-backed storage on Android, expo-secure-store on Expo. Never AsyncStorage, never a plain file, never a log. Ask your backend for the shortest token lifetime you can work with and implement the authExpired round-trip properly — the SDK pauses the form and resumes it the moment you hand back a fresh credential, so a short lifetime costs the user nothing.

Form delegation moves the data plane into your app

Form delegation (onFormOp, React Native only) is opt-in and changes the security picture enough to be worth its own note. With init.formDelegation: true, the portal stops calling its own HTTP endpoints inside /embed/* and instead sends every data operation to your app as a formOp message.

  • Identity becomes yours. The protocol forbids the portal from putting a user id, token or branch into params — those carry only route and product values. Your handler augments the call with whatever identity your backend expects.
  • Form bodies cross the JavaScript bridge. Multipart submissions arrive as ordered entries, with binary parts as base64 dataBase64 strings. Uploaded file content therefore passes through your JS layer; rebuild the body preserving entry order and duplicate keys.
  • There is no fallback. If your handler times out or fails, the portal surfaces a generic error — it must not quietly call its own endpoints while delegation is active. Returning { ok: false, status: 401 } is how you trigger the portal's auth-expired flow.
  • It is unsupported elsewhere, and fails loudly. The native iOS and Android hosts do not implement formOp; the Expo sheet rejects an onFormOp option immediately rather than letting the portal call its own endpoints under the wrong identity.

What this SDK does not do

A reviewer will look for each of these. None of them is implemented, and saying so here is cheaper for everybody than discovering it during a penetration test.

Controls a reviewer may expect, and their actual status
ControlStatusWhere it has to come from instead
Certificate pinning for the page load Not implemented on any platform The system WebView exposes no hook. Pin at the network edge. Android's certificatePinner covers only the manifest fetch and SDK downloads.
Screenshot / screen-recording blocking Not implemented No FLAG_SECURE, no iOS screen-capture handling anywhere in the SDK. Set it on your own hosting activity or window if your policy requires it.
Jailbreak / root / emulator detection Not implemented No integrity attestation of any kind. Use Play Integrity, DeviceCheck or your own RASP before starting a session.
Biometric or re-authentication gate Not implemented The SDK opens a form as soon as it is mounted. Gate the screen in your own navigation.
Token storage or refresh Not implemented, deliberately The SDK holds the token in memory only. Storage, lifetime and refresh are your app's, against the same backend the portal uses.
Scheme allow-listing on openExternal Not implemented Your onOpenExternal hook — return true to intercept.
Content-Security-Policy for the portal page Out of scope A portal-deployment concern, in a different repository and a different review.
Audit logging of user actions Not implemented The SDK emits lifecycle callbacks only. Anything auditable comes from the Core API behind the portal.
Encryption of bridge traffic Not applicable The bridge is in-process between your app and its own WebView; the network hop it protects is TLS.
Deep-link parameter validation Not implemented If a deep link supplies productID or type, validate them before handing them to the SDK — they are untrusted input like any other.
The corresponding short list of what it does guarantee

Credentials never in a URL. Main-frame navigation confined to the portal origin's embed subtree, with sub-frames deliberately exempt. An origin check before every inbound dispatch and every outbound evaluation. HTTPS enforced at config time, with the cleartext hatch dropped by the compiler or the runtime outside a debug build. A version handshake before anything renders. A hardened WebView. Diagnostics that never carry credentials or download headers. A teardown that asks the web layer to clear its persisted auth.

Pre-ship checklist you can actually run

Nine checks against a release candidate. Each one either passes or produces a specific thing to go and fix; none of them requires the SDK's source.

  1. The base URL carries the deploy path

    Against the production portal, not only staging:

    curl -s https://portal.example.com/portal/embed/manifest.json

    It must return JSON with "bridgeProtocolVersion": 1. HTML means the SPA catch-all answered and the prefix is wrong — which also breaks navigation confinement, because the boundary is computed from that same path.

  2. No cleartext hatch in the release configuration

    grep -rn "allowInsecureHttp\|allowInsecureHTTP" src/ ios/ android/
grep -n "NSAllowsArbitraryLoads\|NSExceptionDomains" ios/*/Info.plist
grep -rn "usesCleartextTraffic\|network_security_config" android/app/src/main/

    All three should be empty for the release variant. The flag is inert at runtime in a release build on every platform — but it is still a review finding, and the platform exceptions beside it are not inert at all.

  3. enableLogging comes from a debug constant

    grep -rn "enableLogging" .

    Expect BuildConfig.DEBUG, __DEV__ or your own equivalent — never a literal true. This matters most on Android, where the flag is honoured in a release build.

  4. The token appears in no URL

    Run the app through an intercepting proxy with its CA trusted on a test device, open a form, submit it. The token should appear only in Authorization headers on requests to the portal's own API — never in a request line, query string or fragment, and not at all on GET /embed/manifest.json, which is unauthenticated by design.

  5. Confinement holds

    From inside a form, trigger a link to a URL outside the embed subtree — a different host, or the same host at a path such as /portal/login. The main frame must not move: your onOpenExternal / delegate must fire, or the URL must open outside the WebView. Repeat with a target=_blank link.

  6. Logout really ends the session

    Sign in, open a form, leave the screen, log out of your app, then reopen the form. It must come back anonymous. If it resumes signed in, either destroy never reached the web layer or your own token was not discarded — both are your integration, not the SDK.

  7. Inspect what was left on disk

    Download an attachment from a form, then list the app container: cacheDir/amthal-portal/ on Android, tmp/AmthalPortalDownloads/ on iOS. Those files persist after teardown by design. If your policy forbids that, clear them yourself when the session ends.

  8. Token storage is Keychain or Keystore

    Confirm in your own code, not the SDK's — this is the single most common real finding in an integration review, and the SDK cannot help you with it.

  9. minPortalVersion is set, and its error is handled

    Set it to the oldest portal build you have tested. Present versionIncompatible as "please update the app", not as a retry — it is the one error the SDK never auto-retries, because retrying cannot change the answer.

Reporting a vulnerability

Report privately. Do not open a public GitHub issue.

Emailsecurity@amthalgroup.com
IncludeWhat you found and where — file, endpoint or message type; how to reproduce it; what an attacker could achieve; the SDK version and platform you tested.
ResponseAcknowledgement within two business days, and a disclosure timeline agreed with you before anything is published.
In scopeThis repository: the bridge protocol, the iOS and Android SDKs, the React Native and Expo wrappers.
Out of scopeThe Amthal Client Portal deployment and the Optimum API behind it — operated per tenant; route those through your usual Amthal support contact, which reaches the same team.
Supported versionsSecurity fixes land on the latest minor release. If you are pinned to an older one, say so in the report and the team will advise on the upgrade path.

The normative security rules are section 2.3 of the bridge specification, reproduced and explained on the Bridge protocol page. The configuration options referenced throughout — allowedOrigins, minPortalVersion, enableLogging, the insecure-HTTP hatch and certificatePinner — are documented field by field under Configuration.
